data.title: Slavic gods in the written sources
data.excerpt: At the head of the Slavic pantheon stood, to all appearances, Perún — the ruler of thunder and lightning, god of war and fertility — but our ancestors also knew Veles, Svarog, Dažbog, Mokoš, Svantovít and many more. Five excerpts from written sources, from the Homily of St Gregory to The Tale of Igor’s Campaign, show how the picture of the Slavic gods took shape between the 4th and the 12th century.
data.metaTitle: Slavic gods in the written sources
data.metaDescription: The pantheon of the ancient Slavs in the written sources, headed by the ruler of thunder and lightning: five excerpts from the 4th to the 12th century.

timeline.title: The Homily of Saint Gregory

timeline.title: The Chronicle of John Malalas
timeline.description: The Byzantine chronicler John Malalas describes Svarog and Dažbog within an Egyptian mythological framework.

timeline.title: Nestor’s Tale of Bygone Years

timeline.title: The Tale of Igor’s Campaign
timeline.description: The epic mentions “Dažbog’s grandsons” as a designation of the Rus.

children.text:
I present an excerpt from the very interesting and useful book by Jaromír Slušný: Obraz slovenských dejín, Zborník dokumentov k dejinám Slovenska a Slovákov, Prague 2008.

Our ancestors came to the territory of present-day Slovakia essentially with a system of their own gods that was still developing. At its head stood, to all appearances, the ruler of thunder and lightning, the god of war and fertility Perún, but the Slavs also knew other gods – Veles (Volos), Svarog, Dažbog, Svarožič, Radegast, Mokoš, Rod, Svantovít, Prove, Porevit, Perunič, Triglav, Chors, Stribog, Lada... The development of Slavic iconography is brought closer to us, at least in outline, by the following excerpts from several sources.
1. The Homily of Saint Gregory, 4th century

blocks.text: These Slavs began to make offerings to Rod and the Rožanice before Perún, their god. And before that, offerings were presented to the vampires and the bereginy (protective nymphs). After holy baptism they rejected Perún, revering Christ the Lord our God, but now in hidden places they pray to the accursed god Perún, to Chors, to Mokoš and to the nymphs...
blocks.author: St Gregory of Nazianzus (attributed)
blocks.source: The Homily of Saint Gregory, 4th century (the work was translated into Russian and supplemented around the middle of the 11th century)

children.text: 2. The Chronicle of John Malalas of Antioch, 6th century

blocks.text:
After the death of Feost, whom they also call Svarog, his son the Sun (Helios), also called Dažbog, reigned over the Egyptians... The Sun, then, the ruler, son of Svarog, who is Dažbog, was a strong man... he did not wish to break the law of his father Svarog... As the poet Homer said of him, that Dažbog accused Aphrodite of adultery with Ares... After the death of Dažbog, son of Svarog, Sosis reigned over the Egyptians...
Feost laid down a law for women to marry only one man and to refrain from intercourse with other men, and those who should break this marriage bond he ordered to be punished. For this reason he was called the god Svarog. For before that women lived lewdly with various men who pleased them and were like cattle in their lewdness. When a child was born, the woman said to the one dear to her: “This is your child”, and the man then held a feast and acknowledged it as his own. But Feost abolished this law and ordered that one man should have one wife and that a woman should take only one man; whoever broke this law had to be thrown into a fiery furnace. For this reason he was called Svarog and was revered by the Egyptians... In the time of Feost tongs fell from heaven and iron and weapons began to be forged... for before that they fought with clubs and stones.
blocks.author: John Malalas
blocks.source: The Chronicle of John Malalas of Antioch, 6th century (translated into Old Church Slavonic in the 10th – 11th century)

children.text: John (Ioannes) Malalas (c. 491 – 578) was a Byzantine historian and chronicler born in Antioch. His chronicle was translated into Old Church Slavonic in Bulgaria in the 10th – 11th century and formed one of the foundations of Nestor’s chronicle. Feost = Hephaestus.
3. Helmold of Bosau: Vyhubenie Slovanov pobaltských, 12th century

blocks.text: Having various forms of gods, to whom they assign fields, forests, griefs and pleasures, they acknowledge that one god in the heavens rules over the rest, and is so mighty that he concerns himself only with heavenly matters, while the other gods, having other tasks assigned to them, obey him. From his blood, they say, they sprang, and each of them is the more exalted the closer he is to that god.
blocks.source: Helmold of Bosau (c. 1120 – after 1177): Chronica Slavorum, 12th century

children.text: 4. Nestor: The Tale of Bygone Years, 1113 – 1119

blocks.text: And Prince Vladimir began to reign in Kyiv alone. And he set up idols on the hill outside the tower court: a wooden Perún, and his head of silver, and his moustaches of gold, and Chors, Dažbog and Stribog, Sim, Regl and Mokoš. And he made offerings to them, calling them gods, and they brought their sons and daughters and offered them to the demons, and they defiled the earth with their offerings, and the land of Rus and that hill were defiled with blood... Vladimir then placed Dobrynya in Novgorod. And Dobrynya came to Novgorod, set up an idol (Perún – note by J.S.) above the river Volkhov, and the people of Novgorod made offerings to it as to God.
blocks.author: Nestor

blocks.text: Oleg Gorislavich sowed the seed of wrath, the land was laid waste and plundered by clashes, Dažbog’s grandsons perished in droves. (By the expression “Dažbog’s grandsons” the Rus are meant.)
blocks.author: unknown author
